name: Secondary Hemochromatosis

prevalence.estimate: Variable; depends on underlying condition; affects most chronically transfused patients

criteria.description: Elevated serum ferritin (> 300 ng/mL in men, > 200 ng/mL in women) with identifiable cause
Elevated transferrin saturation (> 45%) or evidence of tissue iron overload
Identifiable secondary cause (chronic transfusions, ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic liver disease, excess oral iron)
Hepatic iron concentration > 3.2 mg/g dry weight on MRI (R2/R2*) or biopsy
Absence of HFE C282Y homozygosity (excluding primary/hereditary hemochromatosis)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Evidence of iron overload (elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation or tissue iron quantification) with an identifiable secondary cause and exclusion of hereditary hemochromatosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Most common causes: chronic red blood cell transfusions (thalassemia major, SCD, MDS), ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic liver disease (hepatitis C, NAFLD, alcoholic liver disease).

common.notes: Bronze diabetes; from iron deposition in skin

occasional.notes: From iron deposition in pancreatic beta cells
From iron deposition in pituitary (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)
Iron cardiomyopathy; more common in transfusional overload

rare.notes: Leading cause of death in transfusional iron overload

laboratory: Serum ferritin markedly elevated (often > 1000 ng/mL in transfusional overload)
Transferrin saturation elevated (>45%); may be lower in inflammation-associated overload
HFE genotyping negative for C282Y homozygosity
imaging: MRI liver R2/R2* (FerriScan): quantifies hepatic iron concentration non-invasively
Cardiac MRI T2*: < 20 ms indicates cardiac iron loading; < 10 ms high-risk for heart failure
Liver ultrasound: may show hepatomegaly, heterogeneous echotexture
genetic: HFE gene testing to exclude hereditary hemochromatosis (C282Y, H63D)
Testing for underlying hemoglobinopathy genes if applicable (HBB for thalassemia)
other: Liver biopsy with Perls Prussian blue staining: demonstrates iron deposition pattern
Endocrine panel: glucose/HbA1c, testosterone, LH/FSH, TSH, cortisol

distinguishingFeatures: Hereditary HH confirmed by HFE C282Y homozygosity or other iron-related gene mutations
Metabolic syndrome-associated hyperferritinemia: transferrin saturation usually normal
Features of metabolic syndrome (obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia)
Hepatic iron is usually mildly elevated
Ferroportin disease may show Kupffer cell iron loading preferentially

redFlags: Cardiac MRI T2* < 10 ms (high risk of fatal arrhythmia or heart failure)
Rapidly declining cardiac function in transfusion-dependent patient
Development of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic liver
Adrenal crisis from iron-mediated adrenal damage
references: Hoffbrand AV, Taher A, Cappellini MD. How I treat transfusional iron overload. Blood. 2012;120(18):3657-3669.
Porter JB, et al. Iron overload and chelation. Int J Hematol. 2011;94(1):56-68.
Bacon BR, et al. Diagnosis and management of hemochromatosis: 2011 practice guideline by AASLD. Hepatology. 2011;54(1):328-343.
